newsitem.title: UK: British stocks seen awaiting U.S. jobs data.
newsitem.headline: British stocks seen awaiting U.S. jobs data.

text.p: A spate of top company results will focus stock market attention in London next week but Wall Street's performance ahead of key U.S. economic data is likely to set the underlying trend, dealers and analysts said on Friday.

Results from the likes of drugs group Glaxo Wellcome , conglomerate BTR and banking giant HSBC will be studied for signs of corporate health in one of the busiest weeks of the year for company results.
Friday's U.S. employment report could provide a key test of market strenth as the recent stock market bull run shows signs of running out of steam on both sides of the Atlantic.

"Next week will be interesting with a lot of company results due," said one senior trader, "but I suspect the market may find it difficult to make any further headway...we have had a good run and the best days could be behind us for the time being."

Markets largely rode out last week's warning of overvalued share prices by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan. The FTSE 100 on Friday closed down just 28.5 points on the week at 4,308.3 after on Tuesday touching a near-record 4,357.9.

Greenspan warned against "exessive optimism" on Wall Street, yet the Dow bounced from an intial tumble, with traders saying there was little to disturb the steady growth, low inflation environment in which shares have risen in recent months.

U.S. mutual funds -- equivalent to British unit trusts -- remain flush with cash and have weighed into the market on any dips. British investment funds are also believed to be running heavy cash positions.
Yet Richard Davidson, European stock market strategist at investment bank Morgan Stanley, said shares could be riding for a fall in coming months.
"We are still bearish," Davidson said, "We are expecting a significant correction at some time over the next six months and it could arrive sooner than that."

He said the trigger for a market retreat could come from an acceleration of growth in Europe -- changing perceptions of interest rate prospects -- a breakdown on moves towards European Monetary Union, or a tightening of rates in the U.S. or Japan.

Perhaps the biggest immediate threat is of a U.S. rate rise -- and any sign of sronger-than-expected growth in next Friday's jobs data could spark fears of higher interest rates in the world's biggest economy.
At British investment bank Robert Fleming, chart analyst Chris Chaitow also said he expected further pressure on Wall Street, in turn depressing shares in London.
"Europe looks better value than the U.S. but the UK is most heavily correlated to Wall Street...we are near the end of the big upward move that started last July."
Chaitow said the yield on the Dow remains below two percent.

"That has happened a few times this century and each time some major disaster has taken place," he said. "People say it's no longer relevant because of factors such as buybacks but in the end they are just ignoring the risk elements."
